subtopic_detail: Empirical antibiotic choice in suspected native valve endocarditis
stem:
You are the medical registrar. A 46 year old man presents with 3 weeks of intermittent fevers, night sweats, and weight loss. He has no prostheses and no intravenous drug use.

He had a dental extraction 5 weeks ago without antibiotic prophylaxis. He has a background of a bicuspid aortic valve with mild aortic regurgitation last echoed 2 years ago.

On examination he has a soft early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge unchanged from prior notes, splinter haemorrhages in two nail beds, and a small painful nodule on the pulp of the left index finger. There is no peripheral oedema and no focal neurology.

Vital signs: pulse 104, blood pressure 122/58, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 97% in room air, temperature 38.4. Three sets of blood cultures have been drawn from separate sites over 90 minutes and sent. Transthoracic echocardiogram has been requested but is not yet available. Urinalysis shows microscopic haematuria. Renal function and electrolytes are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104, BP 122/58, RR 18, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 38.4
data_table.Examination: Early diastolic murmur left sternal edge (unchanged); splinter haemorrhages; painful pulp nodule left index finger; no oedema
data_table.History: Bicuspid aortic valve with mild aortic regurgitation; dental extraction 5 weeks ago without prophylaxis; no prosthetic material; no injecting drug use
data_table.Investigations: Three sets of blood cultures drawn from separate sites over 90 minutes; TTE requested; microscopic haematuria on urinalysis
data_table.Renal: Renal function and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antimicrobial regimen while cultures are pending?

options.text: Vancomycin 25 to 30 mg/kg intravenous loading dose then a targeted maintenance dose alone as monotherapy pending culture and sensitivity results
options.rationale: Vancomycin monotherapy is reserved for suspected native valve endocarditis when severe beta lactam hypersensitivity precludes benzylpenicillin and flucloxacillin, and it is not first line when penicillins are tolerated because streptococcal outcomes are inferior (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Benzylpenicillin 1.8 g intravenously 4 hourly plus flucloxacillin 2 g intravenously 4 hourly plus gentamicin 1 mg/kg intravenously 8 hourly
options.rationale: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic recommends triple therapy with benzylpenicillin, flucloxacillin, and gentamicin as empirical treatment for suspected native valve infective endocarditis in a subacute presentation without risk factors for methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus. The regimen covers viridans streptococci (dental source), Staphylococcus aureus, and enterococci while cultures are pending (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Vancomycin 25 to 30 mg/kg intravenously plus gentamicin 1 mg/kg intravenously 8 hourly plus rifampicin 300 mg orally 8 hourly for the full duration
options.rationale: This is the Therapeutic Guidelines regimen for suspected prosthetic valve endocarditis where staphylococci, including methicillin resistant strains, dominate and biofilm penetration by rifampicin is required; the patient has a native bicuspid valve without prosthetic material (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously daily as monotherapy for community acquired sepsis of unclear source pending the transthoracic echocardiogram result
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone monotherapy does not reliably cover Staphylococcus aureus or enterococci at induction dosing and is not the recommended empirical regimen for suspected native valve endocarditis in Australia; awaiting echo before starting is inappropriate given the clinical picture (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Withhold all antibiotics and repeat three further sets of blood cultures over the next 24 hours before commencing any empirical antimicrobial cover
options.rationale: The three separated culture sets already meet the Duke microbiological criterion pathway; further delay in antimicrobial therapy in a febrile patient with vascular phenomena and a predisposing valve is not justified once adequate cultures have been drawn (Source: Duke criteria (Li et al.); Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: This patient has a subacute febrile illness with a predisposing valve (bicuspid aortic valve with regurgitation), a recent dental source, and peripheral vascular phenomena (splinter haemorrhages, Osler node). Three sets of blood cultures separated in time and space have been taken. Australian empirical therapy for suspected native valve endocarditis is benzylpenicillin plus flucloxacillin plus gentamicin, covering the three dominant pathogen groups until culture results direct narrowing.
key_points: Native valve empirical: benzylpenicillin plus flucloxacillin plus gentamicin.
Prosthetic valve empirical: vancomycin plus gentamicin plus rifampicin.
Do not delay antibiotics after three cultures are drawn.
explanation.pearls: Duke minor criteria met here include predisposition (bicuspid AV), fever, and vascular phenomena. Draw at least three sets of cultures over 60 to 90 minutes from separate sites before empirical therapy, then start Australian triple therapy.

subtopic_detail: Duke criteria interpretation for infective endocarditis
stem:
You are the infectious diseases registrar reviewing a 58 year old woman admitted 3 days ago with fever and malaise. She has a background of a bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement 5 years ago and no injecting drug use.

Two separate blood cultures drawn 4 hours apart have both returned positive for Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly Streptococcus bovis). A transoesophageal echocardiogram today demonstrates a 6 mm mobile vegetation on the prosthetic aortic valve with mild new central aortic regurgitation. She has no janeway lesions, no roth spots, and no glomerulonephritis. Her only minor finding is a temperature of 38.2 on admission.

Examination reveals a soft ejection systolic murmur consistent with her prosthesis and a new soft early diastolic murmur. Peripheral pulses are equal. There are no focal neurological signs.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 128/72, RR 16, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 38.2
data_table.Cultures: Two blood culture sets 4 hours apart both positive for Streptococcus gallolyticus
data_table.Echocardiography: TOE: 6 mm mobile vegetation on prosthetic aortic valve; mild new central aortic regurgitation
data_table.Examination: Soft ejection systolic murmur (prosthesis); new soft early diastolic murmur; no janeway lesions or roth spots

lead_in: How does this case classify under the modified Duke criteria?

options.text: Possible infective endocarditis on the basis of one major criterion and one minor criterion being present in the case
options.rationale: Possible endocarditis requires one major plus one minor, or three minors; both a microbiological major and an echocardiographic major are met here, which upgrades the classification to definite (Source: Duke criteria (Li et al.)).

options.text: Definite infective endocarditis on the basis of one major and three minor criteria being satisfied together in this case
options.rationale: The definite (clinical) category can be reached by one major plus three minors, but here two majors are met directly, so the classification hinges on the two major pathway rather than one major plus three minors (Source: Duke criteria (Li et al.)).

options.text: Rejected diagnosis because prosthetic valve dysfunction alone accounts for both the fever and the new murmur adequately
options.rationale: Rejection requires a firm alternative diagnosis, resolution with fewer than 4 days of antibiotics, or no pathological evidence at surgery or autopsy; positive typical cultures with a prosthetic valve vegetation strongly opposes rejection (Source: Duke criteria (Li et al.)).

options.text: Definite infective endocarditis on the basis of two major criteria being satisfied by the current findings
options.rationale: Two major criteria are met: typical organism (Streptococcus gallolyticus) from two separate blood cultures satisfies the microbiological major criterion, and echocardiographic evidence of a vegetation on the prosthetic valve with new valvular regurgitation satisfies the endocardial involvement major criterion. Two major criteria meet the definite pathological classification (Source: Duke criteria (Li et al.); European Society of Cardiology infective endocarditis guideline).

options.text: Possible infective endocarditis pending a coeliac vascular workup because of the organism identified from the blood culture bottles
options.rationale: Colonoscopy for underlying colorectal neoplasia is an important workup step once endocarditis with Streptococcus gallolyticus is confirmed, but pending colonoscopy does not downgrade the Duke classification which is already definite (Source: Duke criteria (Li et al.); GESA colonoscopy recommendations).

explanation.summary: Modified Duke criteria classify infective endocarditis as definite, possible, or rejected. Two major criteria meet definite. Here, typical organism from two separate cultures and echocardiographic vegetation with new regurgitation both count as majors. Streptococcus gallolyticus mandates colonoscopy for occult colonic pathology, but that workup is independent of the Duke classification.
key_points: Two majors, one major plus three minors, or five minors: definite IE.
Streptococcus gallolyticus: workup for colorectal neoplasia.
Prosthetic valve vegetation is a major echo criterion.
explanation.pearls: Streptococcus gallolyticus bacteraemia should prompt colonoscopy independent of Duke classification because up to a third of cases harbour underlying colonic neoplasia.

subtopic_detail: Surgical referral indication in infective endocarditis
stem:
You are the cardiology registrar covering a 52 year old man on day 6 of intravenous flucloxacillin for definite native mitral valve Staphylococcus aureus endocarditis. He has completed all appropriate dosing and cultures cleared on day 4.

Overnight he developed progressive shortness of breath and orthopnoea. He now has pink frothy sputum and needs to sit upright to breathe. There is no chest pain or focal neurology.

On examination there are bilateral crepitations to the mid zones. A pansystolic murmur at the apex now radiates loudly to the axilla. Transthoracic echocardiogram this morning shows a flail posterior mitral leaflet with severe mitral regurgitation and moderate pulmonary hypertension. Vegetation size is 8 mm.

Vital signs: pulse 118, blood pressure 108/72, respiratory rate 28, SpO2 90% on 4 L nasal prong oxygen, temperature 37.1. He is receiving intravenous furosemide.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 108/72, RR 28, SpO2 90% on 4 L NP, temperature 37.1
data_table.Examination: Bilateral crepitations to mid zones; loud apical pansystolic murmur radiating to axilla
data_table.Echocardiography: Flail posterior mitral leaflet; severe mitral regurgitation; moderate pulmonary hypertension; vegetation 8 mm
data_table.Progress: Day 6 IV flucloxacillin; cultures cleared day 4; receiving IV furosemide

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue intravenous flucloxacillin for a total of 6 weeks and defer surgical review until after antibiotic completion when it will be safer
options.rationale: Delaying surgery in the face of acute severe regurgitation with pulmonary oedema increases mortality; heart failure from valve destruction is a class I early surgical indication (Source: European Society of Cardiology infective endocarditis guideline).
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology infective endocarditis guideline

options.text: Add gentamicin 1 mg/kg intravenously 8 hourly for synergistic activity against Staphylococcus aureus over the next 5 days
options.rationale: Routine addition of aminoglycoside synergy is no longer recommended for native valve Staphylococcus aureus endocarditis because of nephrotoxicity without mortality benefit; the driver of deterioration here is mechanical valve failure (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Commence non invasive ventilation and await repeat echocardiogram in 48 hours before considering surgical referral for the mitral valve
options.rationale: Waiting 48 hours for a repeat echo delays a decision that is already clear on today's echo and clinical presentation; surgery should be discussed with the cardiothoracic team now (Source: European Society of Cardiology infective endocarditis guideline).
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology infective endocarditis guideline

options.text: Urgent cardiothoracic surgical review for consideration of mitral valve surgery on this admission before completing the antibiotic course
options.rationale: Heart failure caused by severe valvular regurgitation from acute valve destruction is the strongest indication for urgent valve surgery during the acute admission and should not wait for antibiotic completion; delay increases mortality (Source: European Society of Cardiology infective endocarditis guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology infective endocarditis guideline

options.text: Change flucloxacillin to vancomycin plus daptomycin for suspected persistent bacteraemia even though cultures were cleared 2 days ago
options.rationale: Cultures were cleared on day 4 so persistent bacteraemia is not the cause; escalation to vancomycin plus daptomycin is not indicated and delays the mechanical intervention needed (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Class I early surgical indications in endocarditis include heart failure from valve destruction, uncontrolled infection despite appropriate therapy, and prevention of embolism (large mobile vegetation >10 mm after an embolic event, or >15 mm even without embolism). Acute severe regurgitation with pulmonary oedema is the most time critical of these.
key_points: Heart failure from valve destruction: class I early surgery.
Do not defer surgery to complete antibiotics.
Aminoglycoside synergy no longer routine in native valve MSSA IE.
explanation.pearls: The three families of surgical indication in IE are heart failure, uncontrolled infection, and prevention of embolism. Heart failure trumps the others for timing.

sources.label: European Society of Cardiology infective endocarditis guideline

subtopic_detail: Empirical therapy in adult community bacterial meningitis
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 34 year old woman presents with 8 hours of severe headache, fever, photophobia, and neck stiffness. She has vomited twice.

She has no known immune compromise, no head trauma, no recent neurosurgery, and no ventricular shunt. She is not pregnant.

Examination reveals full Glasgow coma scale 15, no focal neurology, no papilloedema on fundoscopy, and a positive Brudzinski sign. There is no petechial rash. There is no papilloedema or new onset seizure.

Vital signs: pulse 116, blood pressure 108/62, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 39.5. Intravenous access has been secured and two sets of blood cultures have been drawn. Full blood count and biochemistry have been sent.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 116, BP 108/62, RR 22, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 39.5
data_table.Neurology: GCS 15; no focal deficit; no papilloedema; Brudzinski positive; no seizure
data_table.Access: IV access secured; two sets of blood cultures drawn; FBC and biochemistry sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management step before the lumbar puncture?

options.text: Perform an urgent non contrast CT brain first before any antibiotic administration to exclude a mass lesion causing raised intracranial pressure
options.rationale: CT before LP is only indicated when there is focal neurology, immune compromise, new onset seizure, papilloedema, reduced GCS, or a history of central nervous system disease; none are present, so CT should not delay antibiotic administration (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Give ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously alone and defer dexamethasone until cerebrospinal fluid Gram stain results are back from the pathology laboratory
options.rationale: Dexamethasone must be given with or immediately before the first antibiotic dose to be effective; giving it after antibiotics or waiting for CSF results negates its benefit (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Add benzylpenicillin 1.8 g intravenously 4 hourly to ceftriaxone empirically to cover Listeria monocytogenes in this febrile encephalopathic patient
options.rationale: Listeria cover (benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin) is added in patients over 50 years, pregnancy, immunosuppression, alcohol use disorder, or chronic disease; a 34 year old immunocompetent adult does not need it (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Give dexamethasone 10 mg intravenously with or immediately before ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously and proceed with lumbar puncture as soon as feasible
options.rationale: Australian Therapeutic Guidelines recommend giving dexamethasone (10 mg intravenously) with or just before the first antibiotic dose in adults with suspected bacterial meningitis to reduce neurological sequelae, and empirical ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously covers likely community pathogens. Because there are no features requiring CT before LP (no focal deficit, no immunocompromise, no papilloedema, no seizure, GCS 15), LP can proceed as soon as feasible (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Commence intravenous aciclovir 10 mg/kg 8 hourly first and defer any antibiotic administration until magnetic resonance imaging excludes temporal lobe changes
options.rationale: The presentation is meningitic rather than encephalitic (no altered mental state, seizure, or focal deficit), so empirical aciclovir alone with deferral of antibiotics is inappropriate (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: In adults with suspected community bacterial meningitis and no features mandating CT first, dexamethasone should be given with or immediately before the first antibiotic (ceftriaxone 2 g intravenously) and lumbar puncture performed as soon as feasible. Listeria cover is added only for older, pregnant, or immunocompromised patients.
key_points: Dexamethasone must be given with or immediately before the first antibiotic dose.
CT before LP only if focal neurology, reduced GCS, seizure, papilloedema, or immune compromise.
Add benzylpenicillin for Listeria if >50 years, pregnancy, immunocompromise, or alcohol use disorder.
explanation.pearls: The five CT-before-LP triggers (focal deficit, reduced GCS, new seizure, papilloedema, immunocompromise) are worth memorising. If none present, do not delay LP or antibiotics.

sources.label: van de Beek et al. bacterial meningitis review NEJM

subtopic_detail: HSV encephalitis recognition and treatment
stem:
You are the acute medical registrar. A 41 year old previously well man is brought in by family after 2 days of fever and confusion. Overnight he had a witnessed generalised tonic clonic seizure lasting 90 seconds with a slow postictal recovery.

He has no travel history, no known immune compromise, no illicit drug use, no head trauma, and no ventricular shunt. He takes no regular medications.

On examination he is disoriented to time and place, with expressive dysphasia and no neck stiffness. Cranial nerves and limb power are grossly intact. There is no rash.

Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 128/78, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 97% in room air, temperature 38.9. Non contrast CT brain is normal. Lumbar puncture shows 82 lymphocytes x10^6/L, protein 0.8 g/L (0.15-0.45), glucose 3.6 mmol/L (2.5-4.4, serum glucose 5.4), no organisms on Gram stain, and no red cells suggestive of a traumatic tap. Bacterial cultures and viral polymerase chain reaction have been sent.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 128/78, RR 20, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 38.9
data_table.Neurology: Disoriented; expressive dysphasia; no neck stiffness; witnessed generalised tonic clonic seizure 90 seconds
data_table.CSF: 82 lymphocytes x10^6/L; protein 0.8 g/L (0.15-0.45); glucose 3.6 mmol/L (2.5-4.4); no organisms on Gram stain; no red cells

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Wait for the cerebrospinal fluid polymerase chain reaction result before starting aciclovir to avoid unnecessary intravenous therapy and nephrotoxicity in a low probability case
options.rationale: Delaying aciclovir increases mortality and long term neurological morbidity in herpes simplex encephalitis; empirical therapy is standard while polymerase chain reaction results are pending (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Commence intravenous aciclovir 10 mg/kg 8 hourly and empirical intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g plus dexamethasone 10 mg pending the polymerase chain reaction result
options.rationale: Fever, altered mental state, focal cortical dysfunction (expressive dysphasia), and seizure with a lymphocytic cerebrospinal fluid picture and raised protein are classic for herpes simplex encephalitis. Aciclovir must be started empirically without waiting for polymerase chain reaction because delay increases mortality. Bacterial cover with ceftriaxone plus dexamethasone remains until bacterial meningitis is excluded (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; ANZAN encephalitis guidance).

options.text: Commence intravenous ganciclovir 5 mg/kg 12 hourly as first line empirical therapy for viral encephalitis while awaiting further investigations to return
options.rationale: Ganciclovir targets cytomegalovirus rather than herpes simplex virus, so it is not first line for suspected herpes simplex encephalitis; aciclovir is the empirical drug of choice (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Commence intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g and dexamethasone 10 mg alone without any additional antiviral cover pending further cerebrospinal fluid results in this presentation
options.rationale: Partially treated bacterial meningitis usually shows a lower CSF glucose and higher protein without the focal cortical pattern of dysphasia and seizure; empirical aciclovir must be added when a viral encephalitic picture is present (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Perform urgent contrast enhanced magnetic resonance imaging and defer all antimicrobial therapy until the imaging result returns to guide targeted treatment
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is helpful for confirming temporal lobe involvement but must never delay empirical aciclovir or empirical antibacterial therapy in suspected encephalitis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Suspected viral encephalitis (fever, altered mental state, focal cortical signs, seizure, lymphocytic CSF) is treated with empirical intravenous aciclovir 10 mg/kg 8 hourly. Bacterial cover with ceftriaxone plus dexamethasone continues until bacterial meningitis is excluded. Imaging and polymerase chain reaction must never delay empirical therapy.
key_points: Empirical aciclovir 10 mg/kg IV 8 hourly is time critical.
Continue bacterial cover until meningitis excluded.
MRI temporal lobe involvement and PCR confirm HSV but do not gate therapy.
explanation.pearls: Temporal lobe dysfunction (dysphasia, personality change, olfactory hallucinations) with fever and lymphocytic CSF is HSV encephalitis until proven otherwise. Start aciclovir before you order the MRI.

subtopic_detail: LRINEC and surgical urgency in necrotising soft tissue infection
stem:
You are the surgical registrar reviewing a 58 year old man with type 2 diabetes who presents 18 hours after a minor gardening scratch to the left thigh. He describes pain that has escalated out of proportion to the visible skin change over the last 4 hours.

On examination there is dusky erythema extending from mid thigh to inguinal crease with a small central bulla and crepitus on palpation. He is unable to weight bear and appears diaphoretic. He is on metformin 1 g twice daily and has no antibiotic allergies.

Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 96% in room air, temperature 39.2. Bloods show white cell count 21 x10^9/L (4-11), sodium 130 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 148 micromol/L (60-110), glucose 16 mmol/L, C reactive protein 320 mg/L (0-5), haemoglobin 128 g/L (130-180). Point of care lactate 4.8 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 96/58, RR 26, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 39.2
data_table.Examination: Dusky erythema mid thigh to groin; central bulla; palpable crepitus; unable to weight bear; diaphoretic
data_table.Bloods: WCC 21 x10^9/L; sodium 130 mmol/L; creatinine 148 micromol/L; glucose 16 mmol/L; CRP 320 mg/L; haemoglobin 128 g/L
data_table.Background: T2DM on metformin 1 g twice daily; no antibiotic allergies

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g 6 hourly with fluid resuscitation and observe on the surgical ward with mark border of erythema and repeat review
options.rationale: Marking the border and treating as cellulitis misses the surgical emergency of necrotising infection; antibiotics alone will not control the necrotic process without debridement (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Activate the emergency theatre team for immediate surgical exploration and debridement while concurrent broad spectrum intravenous antibiotics are given
options.rationale: Pain out of proportion, dusky skin with a bulla, palpable crepitus, systemic toxicity, and a high LRINEC score (haemoglobin 128, WCC 21, sodium 130, creatinine 148, glucose 16, CRP 320 exceeds the 8 point threshold) all point to necrotising soft tissue infection. Definitive treatment is surgical exploration and debridement without delay; empirical intravenous antibiotics are adjunctive (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; LRINEC score (Wong et al.)).

options.text: Perform a contrast enhanced computed tomography scan of the thigh to confirm gas in soft tissue before committing to theatre in the middle of the night
options.rationale: Imaging should not delay surgery when clinical necrotising infection is present; palpable crepitus and systemic toxicity are already sufficient to take the patient to theatre (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Refer to hyperbaric oxygen therapy after initial antibiotic administration as the definitive treatment of clostridial gas gangrene in this presentation
options.rationale: Hyperbaric oxygen may have an adjunctive role in some centres but is not the definitive treatment; surgical debridement remains primary and time critical (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Take a punch biopsy of the bulla for bacterial culture and defer surgical exploration until histology confirms the tissue plane involvement definitively
options.rationale: Biopsy delays the definitive intervention and does not change urgency; surgical exploration is both diagnostic and therapeutic in necrotising infection (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection is a surgical emergency. Pain out of proportion, dusky skin with bullae, crepitus, systemic toxicity, and a LRINEC score >=8 are the recognition triad. Definitive therapy is early surgical debridement with concurrent broad spectrum antibiotics. Empirical Australian therapy includes meropenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin (for toxin suppression).
key_points: Necrotising infection is a surgical diagnosis; do not delay for imaging.
LRINEC >=8 has high positive predictive value.
Empirical Australian antibiotics: meropenem + vancomycin + clindamycin.
explanation.pearls: Pain disproportionate to appearance is the earliest and most sensitive clinical clue. If you are debating between imaging and theatre, the answer is theatre.

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis recognition and immediate management
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 38 year old woman with known primary adrenal insufficiency on hydrocortisone 15 mg mane and 5 mg mid afternoon plus fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily presents with 48 hours of vomiting and diarrhoea after a family gastroenteritis outbreak.

She has been unable to keep her usual hydrocortisone down. She feels lightheaded on standing. She has no fever spike and no abdominal peritonism.

On examination she is drowsy but rousable, cool peripherally, and tacky mucous membranes. Abdomen is soft.

Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 82/54, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.4. Point of care venous gas shows pH 7.29, HCO3 16 mmol/L, sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), glucose 3.4 mmol/L, lactate 2.6 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 82/54, RR 22, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.4
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable; cool peripheries; tacky mucous membranes; soft abdomen
data_table.Venous gas: pH 7.29; HCO3 16 mmol/L; sodium 128 mmol/L; potassium 5.6 mmol/L; glucose 3.4 mmol/L; lactate 2.6 mmol/L
data_table.Background: Primary adrenal insufficiency; hydrocortisone 15 mg mane and 5 mg mid afternoon; fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily; 48 hours vomiting and diarrhoea

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenously as a stat dose and commence rapid intravenous normal saline resuscitation with dextrose supplementation
options.rationale: This is adrenal crisis precipitated by gastrointestinal illness in a patient unable to absorb her oral steroid. Immediate management is intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg with volume resuscitation using normal saline and correction of hypoglycaemia with dextrose; do not wait for cortisol assay results (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal crisis guidance; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Draw a random serum cortisol and short synacthen test first and defer hydrocortisone until the biochemical results confirm adrenal insufficiency once received
options.rationale: The diagnosis is already known and the clinical picture is crisis; deferring hydrocortisone for biochemical confirmation risks death and is not required when adrenal insufficiency is established (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Double her usual oral hydrocortisone regimen and give an intravenous antiemetic and observe for 4 hours before deciding on parenteral hormone replacement
options.rationale: Sick day rules of doubling oral hydrocortisone apply to intercurrent illness with intact absorption; established vomiting and hypotension mandate parenteral hydrocortisone (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Give fludrocortisone 100 micrograms intravenously and 2 L intravenous normal saline over 4 hours without any additional glucocorticoid replacement in the meantime
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone has no role in acute crisis at high dose intravenous hydrocortisone because 100 mg hydrocortisone confers sufficient mineralocorticoid effect; fludrocortisone is resumed later with oral maintenance (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Give dexamethasone 4 mg intravenously and then perform a short synacthen test to preserve the diagnostic value of the cortisol assay after the initial dose
options.rationale: Dexamethasone would preserve a cortisol assay but the diagnosis is already known; hydrocortisone is preferred because it provides both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity at 100 mg dose (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis presents with hypotension, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, and hyperkalaemia in a known Addisonian who cannot absorb oral steroid. Immediate treatment is intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg with volume resuscitation and glucose correction. Fludrocortisone is not needed at high dose intravenous hydrocortisone.
key_points: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV immediately; do not wait for assays.
Normal saline resuscitation plus glucose for hypoglycaemia.
Sick day rules (double oral steroid) apply only if absorption is intact.
explanation.pearls: Every Addisonian should carry an emergency hydrocortisone injection kit. The oral doubling rule fails once vomiting starts; escalate to parenteral early.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal crisis position statement

subtopic_detail: Screening test choice for suspected Cushing syndrome
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar. A 42 year old woman is referred with 12 months of central weight gain, easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness on climbing stairs, and new hypertension. She has no known steroid exposure and does not use inhaled or topical steroids.

She has purple abdominal striae wider than 1 cm, thin skin, and a supraclavicular fat pad.

She has no recent shift work, no alcohol use disorder, and no psychiatric illness. She is not on any medications, including oral contraceptives, and she is not pregnant. Her sleep pattern is regular.

Vital signs: pulse 82, blood pressure 158/94, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.7. Baseline biochemistry shows fasting glucose 6.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0). Full blood count and liver enzymes are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82, BP 158/94, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Central adiposity; purple abdominal striae >1 cm wide; thin skin; supraclavicular fat pad; proximal weakness climbing stairs
data_table.History: 12 months insidious onset; no exogenous steroid; regular sleep; no shift work; no alcohol use disorder; no psychiatric illness; not pregnant; no oral contraceptive
data_table.Bloods: Fasting glucose 6.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.5); potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); FBC and liver enzymes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line screening investigation?

options.text: Random plasma cortisol at midday with a random plasma adrenocorticotrophic hormone concentration for immediate interpretation of the axis in the outpatient clinic
options.rationale: Random cortisol has wide diurnal variation and does not screen effectively for hypercortisolism; adrenocorticotrophic hormone measurement is used to determine dependence only after screening confirms Cushing syndrome (Source: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for Cushing syndrome).
source_refs: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for Cushing syndrome

options.text: 8 mg overnight high dose dexamethasone suppression test with an 8am serum cortisol as a first line screen for suspected Cushing syndrome to differentiate causes
options.rationale: High dose dexamethasone suppression is used to differentiate pituitary from ectopic adrenocorticotrophic hormone dependent Cushing syndrome, not as a screening test (Source: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for Cushing syndrome).
source_refs: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for Cushing syndrome

options.text: Corticotrophin releasing hormone stimulation test with inferior petrosal sinus sampling as the initial workup step prior to biochemical confirmation of the diagnosis
options.rationale: Inferior petrosal sinus sampling is reserved for source localisation once adrenocorticotrophic hormone dependent Cushing syndrome is confirmed and pituitary versus ectopic remains unclear; it is not a first screen (Source: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for Cushing syndrome).
source_refs: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for Cushing syndrome

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging pituitary with dedicated dynamic contrast sequences as the first line investigation before biochemical confirmation of hypercortisolism is obtained
options.rationale: Pituitary imaging without biochemical confirmation risks acting on incidentalomas (up to 10% of adults) and is not first line; biochemical confirmation must come first (Source: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for Cushing syndrome).
source_refs: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for Cushing syndrome

options.text: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test with an 8am serum cortisol measurement the following morning as a first screen for endogenous hypercortisolism
options.rationale: The Endocrine Society guideline recommends any one of three first line screens for suspected Cushing syndrome: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression, 24 hour urinary free cortisol on at least two collections, or late night salivary cortisol. All perform similarly for screening; the 1 mg overnight test is the most commonly ordered as an initial screen in the ambulatory setting (Source: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for Cushing syndrome).
source_refs: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for Cushing syndrome

explanation.summary: Three equally valid first line screens for Cushing syndrome exist: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression, 24 hour urinary free cortisol on two collections, and late night salivary cortisol. Adrenocorticotrophic hormone concentration is measured only after biochemical confirmation to determine dependence, and imaging only after biochemistry is diagnostic.
key_points: First line: 1 mg overnight DST, 24h UFC (two collections), or late night salivary cortisol.
ACTH is a dependence classifier, not a screen.
Image only after biochemistry confirms hypercortisolism.
explanation.pearls: Order two of the three screening tests before committing to a diagnosis of Cushing syndrome. Discordant results should trigger repeat testing rather than immediate imaging.
