subtopic_detail: Initial blood pressure control in Stanford type B aortic dissection
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 62 year old man with hypertension and a 30 pack year smoking history presents with sudden onset severe tearing pain between the shoulder blades that started 40 minutes ago.

He has no chest pain radiating to the arm and no focal neurology. Peripheral pulses are equal in both arms and both femoral pulses are palpable. There is no aortic regurgitation on auscultation.

Vital signs: pulse 92 regular, blood pressure 198/112 right arm and 194/108 left arm, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 97% in room air, temperature 36.7. Electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with left ventricular hypertrophy and no acute ischaemic changes. Point of care troponin is negative. CT aortogram shows an intimal flap originating just distal to the left subclavian artery extending to the level of the diaphragm with no branch vessel malperfusion and no aortic root involvement.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 regular, BP 198/112 right arm and 194/108 left arm, RR 22, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Equal pulses; palpable femoral pulses; no aortic regurgitation murmur; no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus with LVH, no ischaemic changes; point of care troponin negative
data_table.Imaging: CTA: intimal flap distal to left subclavian to diaphragm level; no branch malperfusion; no aortic root involvement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological management?

options.text: Intravenous hydralazine 10 mg boluses repeated as required until systolic pressure is below 120 mmHg with beta blockade withheld to preserve compensation
options.rationale: Vasodilator without prior beta blockade causes reflex tachycardia, increased dP/dt, and worsening dissection propagation; beta blockade must precede any vasodilator (Source: European Society of Cardiology aortic disease guideline).
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology aortic disease guideline

options.text: Immediate emergency thoracic endovascular aortic repair without any preceding blood pressure or heart rate control in the emergency department resuscitation bay
options.rationale: Uncomplicated type B dissection is managed medically first; endovascular repair is reserved for complications such as malperfusion, rupture, or refractory pain, and pharmacological control precedes intervention (Source: European Society of Cardiology aortic disease guideline).
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology aortic disease guideline

options.text: Intravenous esmolol infusion titrated to a target heart rate of 60 with intravenous glyceryl trinitrate added if systolic pressure remains above target after rate control
options.rationale: In uncomplicated Stanford type B aortic dissection, medical therapy is first line with tight control of aortic wall shear stress. A beta blocker (esmolol infusion, target heart rate about 60) must be given BEFORE any vasodilator to prevent reflex tachycardia and increased dP/dt; vasodilators (glyceryl trinitrate, sodium nitroprusside) are added to achieve target systolic pressure around 100 to 120 mmHg (Source: European Society of Cardiology aortic disease guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology aortic disease guideline

options.text: Intravenous unfractionated heparin infusion targeting an activated partial thromboplastin time ratio between 2 and 3 while waiting for a vascular surgical opinion
options.rationale: Anticoagulation is contraindicated in acute aortic dissection because it increases the risk of catastrophic haemorrhage from the false lumen (Source: European Society of Cardiology aortic disease guideline).
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology aortic disease guideline

options.text: Sublingual glyceryl trinitrate 400 micrograms with oral amlodipine 10 mg and observe blood pressure response over the next hour before intravenous escalation
options.rationale: Oral and sublingual therapy is inadequate for the rapid tight control needed in dissection; intravenous titratable agents are required (Source: European Society of Cardiology aortic disease guideline).
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology aortic disease guideline

explanation.summary: Uncomplicated Stanford type B dissection (originating distal to left subclavian, no malperfusion or rupture) is managed medically with tight control of aortic wall stress. Beta blockade (esmolol infusion, target heart rate 60) always precedes any vasodilator to avoid reflex tachycardia. Then add a vasodilator to reach systolic 100 to 120 mmHg.
key_points: Beta blocker first (esmolol), then vasodilator.
Target heart rate 60; systolic 100 to 120 mmHg.
Endovascular repair reserved for complications.
explanation.pearls: The rule beta first, vasodilator second exists because arterial dilation without heart rate control increases dP/dt and propagates the flap. Never open the tap before you close the valve.

sources.label: European Society of Cardiology aortic disease guideline

subtopic_detail: AAA surveillance interval per Australian vascular guidance
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 68 year old asymptomatic ex smoker attends for a review. An abdominal ultrasound was ordered after an incidental finding on a renal scan showed a fusiform infrarenal aortic dilatation of 4.6 cm anteroposterior diameter at the maximum point.

He has controlled hypertension on perindopril and a total cholesterol of 4.8 mmol/L on atorvastatin. He has no back or abdominal pain, no leg pain on walking, and no family history of aortic dissection. He gave up smoking 10 years ago and has no ischaemic heart disease.

Vital signs: pulse 68 regular, blood pressure 132/78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.6. Peripheral pulses are equal. There is a soft mid abdominal pulsation without bruit or tenderness.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68 regular, BP 132/78, RR 14, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Ultrasound: Fusiform infrarenal AAA 4.6 cm anteroposterior maximum diameter
data_table.Symptoms: Asymptomatic; no back or abdominal pain; no leg claudication
data_table.History: Ex smoker (quit 10 years ago); controlled hypertension; on atorvastatin; no family history aortic dissection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate follow up plan?

options.text: Repeat abdominal ultrasound surveillance in 6 months and continue optimising cardiovascular risk factors with cessation counselling reinforcement at each attendance
options.rationale: The Australian and New Zealand Society for Vascular Surgery and international guidance recommend ultrasound surveillance every 6 months for infrarenal AAA between 4.5 and 5.4 cm in men, and referral for repair when diameter reaches 5.5 cm, expansion exceeds 1 cm in a year, or symptoms develop (Source: ANZSVS AAA guidance; Society for Vascular Surgery AAA guideline).

options.text: Refer for open surgical repair of the aneurysm without further delay because the diameter of 4.6 cm crosses the surgical threshold defined by the vascular surgical society
options.rationale: The elective repair threshold in men is 5.5 cm (in women often 5.0 cm); 4.6 cm continues on surveillance rather than proceeding to repair (Source: ANZSVS AAA guidance).

options.text: Repeat ultrasound in 12 months and refer only if diameter reaches 5.5 cm or symptoms develop; no interval change to surveillance based on current findings
options.rationale: Annual surveillance is appropriate for smaller aneurysms (3.0 to 3.9 cm); at 4.5 to 5.4 cm the interval is 6 monthly because growth risk is higher (Source: ANZSVS AAA guidance).

options.text: Repeat computed tomography aortogram in 3 months with contrast for detailed anatomical assessment before any decision on further surveillance interval is made now
options.rationale: Ultrasound is the surveillance modality of choice because it avoids radiation and contrast; CTA is reserved for pre operative planning once repair is indicated (Source: ANZSVS AAA guidance).

options.text: Commence beta blockade with metoprolol 25 mg twice daily specifically to reduce aortic wall stress and slow the rate of aneurysm expansion in the surveillance period
options.rationale: There is no consistent evidence that beta blockade slows AAA expansion; risk factor optimisation (blood pressure control, statin, cessation) is the medical mainstay (Source: ANZSVS AAA guidance).

explanation.summary: AAA surveillance intervals: 3.0 to 3.9 cm every 24 months; 4.0 to 4.4 cm every 12 months; 4.5 to 5.4 cm every 6 months (some centres 3 monthly at upper range). Repair thresholds: 5.5 cm in men, 5.0 cm in women, or rapid expansion (>1 cm per year), or symptoms.
key_points: 6 monthly ultrasound for 4.5 to 5.4 cm in men.
Elective repair at 5.5 cm men, 5.0 cm women, rapid growth, or symptoms.
Ultrasound preferred over CT for surveillance.
explanation.pearls: Rapid expansion (>1 cm per year) is an independent trigger for repair even below the diameter threshold. Ask about family history of dissection; it lowers the repair threshold.

sources.label: Society for Vascular Surgery AAA guideline

subtopic_detail: Massive transfusion protocol activation criteria
stem:
You are the trauma team leader. A 34 year old man is brought in after a high speed motor vehicle collision. He has a distended tender abdomen with a suspected splenic injury and a closed left femur fracture.

He has received 1 L crystalloid in the pre hospital setting. On arrival he remains hypotensive despite resuscitation.

Vital signs: pulse 138, blood pressure 78/48, respiratory rate 30, SpO2 96% on 15 L non rebreather, temperature 35.2. Point of care venous gas: pH 7.18, HCO3 14 mmol/L, lactate 6.8 mmol/L. Focussed assessment sonography for trauma is positive in the right upper quadrant and pelvis. Initial haemoglobin 88 g/L (130-180). Estimated blood loss so far is more than 30% of blood volume with ongoing haemorrhage suspected. Antifibrinolytic drug not yet given.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138, BP 78/48, RR 30, SpO2 96% on 15 L NRB, temperature 35.2
data_table.Investigations: FAST positive RUQ and pelvis; Hb 88 g/L (130-180)
data_table.Estimated loss: >30% blood volume with ongoing haemorrhage suspected
data_table.Interventions: Pre hospital 1 L crystalloid; antifibrinolytic not yet given

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in resuscitation?

options.text: Continue crystalloid resuscitation to at least 3 L before commencing any blood product transfusion in order to preserve blood bank stocks during the initial period
options.rationale: Crystalloid resuscitation in massive haemorrhage worsens dilutional coagulopathy and mortality; early blood product resuscitation is preferred (Source: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines

options.text: Transfuse packed red cells alone at 4 units per hour and reassess coagulation after 4 units before considering fresh frozen plasma and platelets addition later
options.rationale: Red cell only resuscitation without concurrent plasma and platelets worsens trauma induced coagulopathy; a balanced ratio is standard for massive transfusion (Source: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines

options.text: Give recombinant activated factor VII 90 micrograms/kg first line as a haemostatic adjunct before any blood component therapy is administered in this resuscitation
options.rationale: Recombinant factor VIIa is not first line, carries thrombotic risk, and is reserved for refractory haemorrhage after balanced resuscitation and surgical control (Source: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines

options.text: Give an antifibrinolytic drug 24 hours after injury only if the patient continues to require blood product transfusion at that time rather than in the immediate resuscitation period
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid must be given within 3 hours of injury to reduce mortality; benefit disappears and harm may increase after that window (Source: CRASH-2 trial).

options.text: Activate the institutional massive transfusion protocol with balanced red cells, plasma, and platelets in a 1:1:1 ratio and give tranexamic acid 1 g intravenously now
options.rationale: The National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines and CRASH-2 evidence support massive transfusion protocol activation with a 1:1:1 ratio for haemorrhagic shock, plus tranexamic acid 1 g intravenously within 3 hours of injury followed by an 8 hour infusion; benefit is greatest when given within the first hour (Source: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines; CRASH-2 trial).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines

explanation.summary: Haemorrhagic shock in trauma with ongoing bleeding warrants massive transfusion protocol activation with a balanced 1:1:1 ratio of red cells, plasma, and platelets, plus tranexamic acid 1 g intravenously within 3 hours of injury (followed by an 8 hour infusion). Crystalloid resuscitation worsens coagulopathy and should be minimised.
key_points: 1:1:1 ratio red cells : plasma : platelets.
TXA 1 g within 3 hours (then 1 g over 8 h infusion).
Give ionised calcium after every 4 units of red cells.
explanation.pearls: The lethal triad in trauma is hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy. Warm the fluids, correct calcium, and give TXA early.

sources.label: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Warfarin reversal in major bleeding
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 76 year old man on warfarin for mechanical mitral valve replacement presents 2 hours after a witnessed fall down 5 stairs. He has a new right sided hemiparesis and GCS 12.

Non contrast CT brain shows a 25 mL right frontal intraparenchymal haemorrhage with 4 mm midline shift. There is no intraventricular extension.

His last INR 1 week ago was 2.6 (target 2.5-3.5). Current INR is 3.4. He weighs 82 kg. Renal function is within normal limits and he has no known heparin allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 168/94, RR 18, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.CT brain: 25 mL right frontal intraparenchymal haemorrhage; 4 mm midline shift; no intraventricular extension
data_table.Weight: 82 kg; normal renal function; no heparin allergy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate reversal strategy?

options.text: Give intravenous vitamin K 10 mg alone and await 12 hourly INR checks before considering further reversal with clotting factor concentrates or fresh frozen plasma products
options.rationale: Vitamin K alone takes 6 to 24 hours for effect and is inadequate for major bleeding; PCC gives immediate factor replacement (Source: HSANZ ASTH warfarin reversal consensus).

options.text: Give fresh frozen plasma 4 units alone as first line reversal without prothrombin complex concentrate to avoid the thrombotic risk of concentrated factor products in this patient
options.rationale: PCC provides more rapid and complete reversal, avoids volume overload, and is now preferred over fresh frozen plasma for warfarin associated major bleeding (Source: HSANZ ASTH warfarin reversal consensus).

options.text: Give recombinant activated factor VII as first line reversal because it acts faster than any other agent and provides complete correction of the coagulopathy on its own
options.rationale: Recombinant factor VIIa is not first line for warfarin reversal and carries higher thrombotic risk; PCC replaces the deficient factors that warfarin depletes (Source: HSANZ ASTH warfarin reversal consensus).

options.text: Withhold reversal entirely and observe with 6 hourly INR trends because the current value is close to therapeutic range for the mechanical valve indication
options.rationale: Even therapeutic INR contributes to expansion of intracranial haemorrhage; reversal is mandatory in major intracranial bleeding on warfarin regardless of INR being within target (Source: HSANZ ASTH warfarin reversal consensus).

options.text: Give prothrombin complex concentrate at a weight based dose according to INR plus intravenous vitamin K 10 mg with immediate neurosurgical referral for review
options.rationale: The National Blood Authority and Australasian Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis guidance for warfarin associated intracranial haemorrhage recommends prothrombin complex concentrate (25 to 50 units/kg based on INR) plus intravenous vitamin K 5 to 10 mg for durable reversal, with immediate neurosurgical involvement. Vitamin K provides sustained reversal after PCC wanes (Source: HSANZ ASTH warfarin reversal consensus; National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Warfarin associated intracranial haemorrhage is reversed with prothrombin complex concentrate (dose by INR and weight) plus intravenous vitamin K 5 to 10 mg. PCC gives immediate correction; vitamin K provides sustained reversal after PCC wanes. Fresh frozen plasma is second line if PCC is unavailable.
key_points: PCC + IV vitamin K is first line for warfarin ICH.
FFP is second line only if PCC unavailable.
Reversal even at therapeutic INR when bleeding is major.
explanation.pearls: Restart of anticoagulation after ICH in a mechanical valve is a specialist decision, typically 1 to 2 weeks after haemostasis, weighing thromboembolic against rebleed risk.

sources.label: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines

subtopic_detail: DOAC reversal choice in major bleeding
stem:
You are the medical registrar. A 72 year old woman on apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation presents with progressive severe headache and left sided weakness over 2 hours.

Her last apixaban dose was 6 hours ago. She has no other anticoagulation, no antiplatelet therapy, and no chronic kidney disease. She has never had a bleeding event before.

On examination GCS is 13 with a dense left hemiplegia. Non contrast CT brain shows a 30 mL right basal ganglia intracerebral haemorrhage with intraventricular extension into the third ventricle.

Vital signs: pulse 92, blood pressure 182/104, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.5. She weighs 68 kg. Renal function is within normal limits. Coagulation screen is otherwise within normal limits with an INR of 1.1.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 182/104, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.5
data_table.CT brain: 30 mL right basal ganglia haemorrhage with intraventricular extension into third ventricle
data_table.Drug history: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily; last dose 6 hours ago; no other anticoagulant or antiplatelet

lead_in: What is the most appropriate specific reversal option to request?

options.text: Idarucizumab given as two 2.5 g intravenous boluses no more than 15 minutes apart as a specific antidote for this direct oral anticoagulant currently in use
options.rationale: Idarucizumab is the specific antidote for dabigatran (direct thrombin inhibitor), not for apixaban (factor Xa inhibitor) (Source: HSANZ ASTH DOAC reversal guidance).

options.text: Andexanet alfa given as an intravenous bolus followed by a 2 hour maintenance infusion at a low or high dose regimen based on last apixaban dose and timing
options.rationale: Andexanet alfa is the specific reversal agent for direct factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban) and reduces anti Xa activity within minutes. Dose depends on last dose amount and interval; four factor prothrombin complex concentrate is a reasonable alternative if andexanet is unavailable (Source: HSANZ ASTH DOAC reversal guidance).

options.text: Protamine sulfate infused intravenously over 10 minutes as neutralising therapy for direct oral anticoagulants in the setting of a major intracranial bleeding event
options.rationale: Protamine reverses unfractionated heparin (partially reverses low molecular weight heparin) and has no role in reversing direct oral anticoagulants (Source: HSANZ ASTH DOAC reversal guidance).

options.text: Fresh frozen plasma at 15 mL/kg given as first line specific reversal therapy for direct oral anticoagulant related intracranial haemorrhage in the emergency department
options.rationale: Fresh frozen plasma does not reverse the pharmacological activity of direct oral anticoagulants because it does not neutralise the drug; specific antidote or PCC is required (Source: HSANZ ASTH DOAC reversal guidance).

options.text: Intravenous vitamin K 10 mg given as first line reversal because the patient is on an oral anticoagulant with rapid onset of INR correction observed on repeat testing
options.rationale: Vitamin K reverses warfarin by restoring vitamin K dependent factor synthesis; it has no effect on direct oral anticoagulants that act downstream of factor synthesis (Source: HSANZ ASTH DOAC reversal guidance).

explanation.summary: Match the antidote to the drug: idarucizumab for dabigatran, andexanet alfa for apixaban and rivaroxaban (four factor PCC alternative if unavailable), protamine for unfractionated heparin, and vitamin K plus PCC for warfarin. Fresh frozen plasma is not effective for DOAC reversal.
key_points: Andexanet alfa reverses apixaban and rivaroxaban.
Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran.
FFP does not reverse DOACs; PCC is the alternative when andexanet unavailable.
explanation.pearls: Time from last dose matters. If last apixaban dose was >18 hours ago with normal renal function, drug concentration may be low enough that reversal offers little benefit.

subtopic_detail: Mixed acid base and anion gap interpretation
stem:
You are the intensive care registrar. A 58 year old man with type 2 diabetes and chronic alcohol use presents with 3 days of vomiting after a heavy binge. He last ate 36 hours ago.

He has no diarrhoea. He takes metformin 1 g twice daily and no other regular medications. He has no known chronic liver disease.

On examination he is drowsy but rousable and his breath is fruity. He is deeply tachypnoeic with Kussmaul respirations. Peripheries are cool. Abdomen is soft with epigastric tenderness.

Vital signs: pulse 122, blood pressure 106/72, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 99% in room air, temperature 36.4. Arterial blood gas on room air: pH 7.28, pCO2 22 mmHg, pO2 108 mmHg, HCO3 10 mmol/L. Sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), chloride 92 mmol/L (95-110), glucose 14 mmol/L, ketones 5.2 mmol/L, lactate 3.1 mmol/L, albumin 34 g/L (35-50).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122, BP 106/72, RR 32, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.4
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable; fruity breath; Kussmaul respirations; cool peripheries; epigastric tenderness
data_table.ABG: pH 7.28; pCO2 22 mmHg; pO2 108 mmHg; HCO3 10 mmol/L
data_table.Biochemistry: Sodium 138; potassium 3.4 (3.5-5.0); chloride 92 (95-110); glucose 14; ketones 5.2; lactate 3.1; albumin 34 (35-50)
data_table.History: 3 days vomiting after heavy alcohol binge; last ate 36 hours ago; metformin 1 g bd

lead_in: Which best characterises the acid base disturbance?

options.text: Pure high anion gap metabolic acidosis due to alcoholic ketoacidosis with appropriate compensation for the fall in bicarbonate and no additional disorder identified in this case
options.rationale: Delta ratio of 2.0 indicates a coexisting metabolic alkalosis from vomiting; pure acidosis would have a delta ratio between 1 and 2 (Source: Nicholas Levine acid base handbook).

options.text: Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory alkalosis compensation from diarrhoea induced bicarbonate loss and hyperventilation from the acid load in this presentation
options.rationale: Anion gap is raised, and the patient has no diarrhoea; the picture is a high not a normal gap acidosis (Source: Nicholas Levine acid base handbook).

options.text: High anion gap metabolic acidosis with concurrent metabolic alkalosis and appropriate respiratory compensation for the underlying metabolic disturbance seen in this case
options.rationale: Anion gap corrected for albumin is 138 - (92+10) = 36, and albumin correction adds about 4 to give 40 (raised, normal 12). Expected pCO2 by Winter's formula is 1.5 x 10 + 8 = 23 (measured 22, appropriate). Delta ratio (delta gap 40-12=28 divided by delta bicarbonate 24-10=14) is 2.0, above 2 indicating a coexisting metabolic alkalosis from prolonged vomiting. All three coexist (Source: Nicholas Levine acid base handbook; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Primary respiratory alkalosis with metabolic compensation because tachypnoea has driven the pCO2 down and generated a low bicarbonate in this vomiting deteriorating patient
options.rationale: In primary respiratory alkalosis the pH is above 7.45; this patient's pH is 7.28, so the primary disturbance is metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation (Source: Nicholas Levine acid base handbook).

options.text: Compensated respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation from renal bicarbonate retention in a chronically hypercarbic patient with newly progressive respiratory failure
options.rationale: Respiratory acidosis has a high pCO2; this patient's pCO2 is 22 which reflects respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis, not a primary respiratory disorder (Source: Nicholas Levine acid base handbook).

explanation.summary: Systematic acid base interpretation: 1) primary disturbance from pH and pCO2 and HCO3; 2) calculate anion gap (Na - (Cl + HCO3)) and correct for albumin; 3) check Winter's formula compensation for metabolic acidosis (pCO2 = 1.5xHCO3 + 8); 4) calculate delta ratio to identify additional metabolic disturbances. Here: HAGMA (ketoacidosis + lactic), appropriate respiratory compensation, and coexisting metabolic alkalosis (vomiting) revealed by delta ratio >2.
key_points: Correct anion gap for albumin (add 2.5 per 10 g/L below 40).
Winter's formula: expected pCO2 = 1.5 x HCO3 + 8 (+/- 2).
Delta ratio: <1 concurrent NAGMA; 1-2 pure HAGMA; >2 coexisting metabolic alkalosis.
explanation.pearls: Alcoholic ketoacidosis often coexists with vomiting induced alkalosis, so the delta ratio is characteristically raised. Watch for hypokalaemia and hypophosphataemia during dextrose and thiamine loaded rehydration.

subtopic_detail: Opioid rotation ratio from oral morphine to oral hydromorphone
stem:
You are the palliative care registrar. A 62 year old woman with metastatic pancreatic cancer has been on slow release oral morphine 60 mg twice daily for background pain, with morphine 10 mg oral immediate release breakthrough doses. She uses about 4 breakthrough doses per day for adequate control.

Over the last week she has developed persistent nausea and myoclonus that her general practitioner considers to be a partial opioid neurotoxicity picture. She is otherwise cognitively intact. Renal function is within normal limits and she has no allergies.

You plan to rotate her to oral hydromorphone using an equianalgesic conversion factor of 5 (5 mg oral morphine equivalent to 1 mg oral hydromorphone) and then reduce by one third for incomplete cross tolerance and the neurotoxicity picture. She has no barrier to oral intake and no fentanyl patch currently in situ.

data_table.Current opioid: Slow release morphine 60 mg oral twice daily; immediate release morphine 10 mg oral breakthrough approximately 4 doses per day
data_table.Adverse effects: Persistent nausea and myoclonus (partial opioid neurotoxicity)
data_table.Function: Cognitively intact; oral route available; no fentanyl patch in situ
data_table.Conversion plan: Oral hydromorphone; oral morphine to oral hydromorphone conversion factor of 5; reduce by one third for incomplete cross tolerance and neurotoxicity

lead_in: What is the most appropriate new hydromorphone regimen?

options.text: Slow release hydromorphone 16 mg oral twice daily with immediate release hydromorphone 4 mg oral breakthrough as required for pain
options.rationale: This is the direct equianalgesic conversion without reduction for incomplete cross tolerance; it risks overdose after rotation and does not address the neurotoxicity driver (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Slow release hydromorphone 32 mg oral twice daily with immediate release hydromorphone 8 mg oral breakthrough as required for pain
options.rationale: This uses the direct oral morphine dose in mg as hydromorphone dose (no conversion factor applied); it is a 5 fold overdose and is dangerous (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Slow release hydromorphone 4 mg oral twice daily with immediate release hydromorphone 1 mg oral breakthrough as required for pain
options.rationale: This under doses (5 mg/day) relative to the appropriate rotated dose (about 22 mg/day) and would leave uncontrolled pain (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Continue slow release morphine at 60 mg oral twice daily and add regular metoclopramide with clonazepam for the myoclonus in preference to opioid rotation
options.rationale: Persistent opioid neurotoxicity is an indication for opioid rotation rather than symptomatic layering; symptom drugs treat the surface without addressing the drug driver (Source: Palliative Care Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Slow release hydromorphone 8 mg oral twice daily with immediate release hydromorphone 2 mg oral breakthrough as required for pain
options.rationale: Total daily oral morphine is 60 x 2 + 10 x 4 = 160 mg. Converted to oral hydromorphone at 5:1 gives 32 mg/day, reduced by one third for cross tolerance and neurotoxicity gives about 22 mg/day, rounded to 16 mg/day (8 mg BD slow release) with 2 mg immediate release breakthrough (approximately one sixth to one tenth of the 24 hour dose per breakthrough per Palliative Care Australia and AMH guidance) (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; Palliative Care Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Opioid rotation for neurotoxicity: sum the 24 hour oral morphine equivalent, apply the equianalgesic ratio (oral morphine to oral hydromorphone approximately 5:1), then reduce by 25 to 50% for incomplete cross tolerance. Set breakthrough at one sixth to one tenth of the 24 hour dose.
key_points: Sum total 24 hour oral morphine equivalent before conversion.
Oral morphine to oral hydromorphone ratio approximately 5:1.
Reduce by 25 to 50% for incomplete cross tolerance and neurotoxicity.
explanation.pearls: Renal impairment shifts the balance further toward reduction because active morphine metabolites (M6G, M3G) accumulate and worsen neurotoxicity. Hydromorphone has active metabolites too but at lower risk.

subtopic_detail: Anticipatory prescribing for terminal secretions
stem:
You are the palliative care registrar in a community setting. A 78 year old man with end stage heart failure has entered the terminal phase and is being cared for at home. He is deeply drowsy and no longer taking oral fluids.

In the last 4 hours he has developed audible upper airway secretions that his wife finds distressing. He does not appear distressed himself and is not tachypnoeic. There are no crackles suggestive of pulmonary oedema on the last clinician examination this morning.

He has a subcutaneous butterfly in situ and is receiving small doses of subcutaneous morphine for background dyspnoea. He has no glaucoma, no urinary retention, and no bowel obstruction. He is not on regular anticholinergic medications.

data_table.Setting: Home; terminal phase; deeply drowsy; not taking oral fluids
data_table.Symptom: Audible upper airway secretions for 4 hours distressing spouse; patient not distressed; not tachypnoeic
data_table.Examination: No pulmonary oedema crackles this morning
data_table.Access: Subcutaneous butterfly in situ; receiving subcutaneous morphine for background dyspnoea
data_table.Contraindications: No glaucoma; no urinary retention; no bowel obstruction; no regular anticholinergic

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticipatory prescription?

options.text: Glycopyrronium 200 to 400 micrograms subcutaneously as required with a 1 hour minimum interval and offer explanation to the spouse about repositioning and drying secretions
options.rationale: Palliative Care Therapeutic Guidelines recommend an antimuscarinic (glycopyrronium 200 to 400 micrograms subcutaneously PRN, or hyoscine butylbromide 20 mg subcutaneously PRN) for terminal secretions, combined with repositioning and family explanation because established secretions rarely fully clear once formed. Glycopyrronium is preferred where blood brain barrier crossing (delirium) is a concern (Source: Palliative Care Therapeutic Guidelines; Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Frusemide 40 mg subcutaneously stat with an intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion at home to treat presumed acute pulmonary oedema in this end stage heart failure patient
options.rationale: The examination this morning did not identify pulmonary oedema; audible upper airway secretions in the terminal phase are secretion pooling, not cardiogenic (Source: Palliative Care Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Insert an oropharyngeal suction catheter and perform deep suctioning every 2 hours to remove all secretions and admit to inpatient palliative care unit for closer monitoring
options.rationale: Deep suctioning is distressing and often ineffective; it is not routine in terminal secretions and is inconsistent with the goal of comfort at home (Source: Palliative Care Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg every 4 hours regularly and add ipratropium 500 micrograms nebulised every 6 hours to open airway calibre in this terminal phase heart failure patient
options.rationale: Bronchodilators do not address pooled upper airway secretions and expose the patient to unnecessary intervention; the target is drying of secretions, not bronchodilation (Source: Palliative Care Therapeutic Guidelines).

options.text: Increase the subcutaneous morphine dose by 50% and add regular subcutaneous midazolam to sedate the patient because the family finds the secretions distressing to hear
options.rationale: Escalating opioid or benzodiazepine without a symptom driver in the patient is inappropriate; the target of intervention is the secretion, not the patient's conscious state, and the family need explanation and repositioning support (Source: Palliative Care Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: Terminal upper airway secretions (death rattle) are managed with an antimuscarinic (glycopyrronium or hyoscine butylbromide subcutaneously PRN), repositioning, and explanation to family. Established secretions rarely resolve fully. Suctioning is not routine. Bronchodilators, diuretics, and dose escalation of sedatives are not first line for secretion pooling.
key_points: Glycopyrronium 200 to 400 micrograms SC PRN or hyoscine butylbromide 20 mg SC PRN.
Reposition on the side and explain to family early.
Do not increase opioid or midazolam for family distress alone.
explanation.pearls: Anticipatory prescriptions in the terminal phase always include an opioid (dyspnoea/pain), an antiemetic, an anxiolytic, and an antimuscarinic secretion drug. Prescribe them proactively so the community nurse or family can act without delay.

subtopic_detail: Chronic Addison disease sick day rules
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A 44 year old man with autoimmune Addison disease on hydrocortisone 15 mg mane and 5 mg mid afternoon plus fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily attends for advice.

He rang because he has developed a 24 hour history of fevers to 38.6 and a productive cough that the practice nurse has assessed by phone as likely uncomplicated community acquired lower respiratory tract infection. He is tolerating oral fluids and food normally and has no vomiting. He has a written adrenal insufficiency care plan and an emergency hydrocortisone kit at home. He has not had any surgery planned in the near future.

data_table.Symptoms: 24 hours fever to 38.6; productive cough; no vomiting; tolerating oral intake
data_table.Assessment: Practice nurse phone review: likely uncomplicated community acquired lower respiratory tract infection
data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 118/76, RR 18, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 38.6
data_table.Regular therapy: Hydrocortisone 15 mg mane and 5 mg mid afternoon; fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily
data_table.Preparedness: Written adrenal insufficiency care plan and emergency hydrocortisone injection kit at home

lead_in: What is the most appropriate glucocorticoid advice to give now?

options.text: Continue fludrocortisone unchanged and double the total daily oral hydrocortisone dose for the duration of the febrile illness and until 24 hours after resolution
options.rationale: Standard sick day rules for chronic adrenal insufficiency in an oral tolerating patient with fever above 38 are to double the total daily oral hydrocortisone (typical minimum 20 mg per dose for a full illness day) for the duration of the febrile illness and continue until 24 hours after resolution. Fludrocortisone is left unchanged when hydrocortisone is at high replacement doses (Source: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for primary adrenal insufficiency).
source_refs: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for primary adrenal insufficiency

options.text: Give a 100 mg intramuscular hydrocortisone injection from the emergency kit at home now and attend the emergency department urgently for further parenteral care
options.rationale: The emergency hydrocortisone injection is reserved for vomiting or shock or when oral therapy cannot be tolerated; this patient tolerates oral intake and can double his oral dose (Source: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for primary adrenal insufficiency).
source_refs: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for primary adrenal insufficiency

options.text: Continue his usual daily hydrocortisone dose unchanged and add an oral antibiotic for the respiratory tract infection with no additional glucocorticoid coverage during the illness
options.rationale: Failing to increase glucocorticoid dose during a febrile illness risks progression to adrenal crisis; sick day dosing is essential in chronic adrenal insufficiency (Source: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for primary adrenal insufficiency).
source_refs: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for primary adrenal insufficiency

options.text: Quadruple the daily hydrocortisone dose to 80 mg total daily for the duration of the illness in addition to increasing his fludrocortisone dose to 200 micrograms daily
options.rationale: Doubling is the standard sick day rule for febrile illness; quadrupling is reserved for major surgery or severe illness. Fludrocortisone need not be increased when hydrocortisone is high because at that dose it has mineralocorticoid activity (Source: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for primary adrenal insufficiency).
source_refs: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for primary adrenal insufficiency

options.text: Switch to oral prednisolone 25 mg once daily for the duration of the acute illness because the longer half life provides more stable cover than divided hydrocortisone doses
options.rationale: Hydrocortisone is preferred to prednisolone in chronic adrenal insufficiency because it more closely mimics physiological diurnal cortisol replacement; switching agents during acute illness adds risk without benefit (Source: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for primary adrenal insufficiency).
source_refs: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for primary adrenal insufficiency

explanation.summary: Sick day rules for chronic adrenal insufficiency: for fever above 38 or moderate intercurrent illness with intact oral absorption, double the total daily oral hydrocortisone until 24 hours after resolution. For vomiting, diarrhoea, or shock, use intramuscular emergency hydrocortisone and attend hospital. Major surgery requires 100 mg IV plus infusion.
key_points: Fever above 38 with intact absorption: double oral hydrocortisone.
Vomiting or shock: intramuscular hydrocortisone injection and emergency department.
Fludrocortisone unchanged when hydrocortisone dose is high.
explanation.pearls: Every Addisonian should carry a MedicAlert bracelet, an emergency hydrocortisone kit, and a written care plan. Rehearse the injection technique at every review.

sources.label: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for primary adrenal insufficiency

subtopic_detail: Stanford type A dissection recognition
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 58 year old woman with poorly controlled hypertension presents with 30 minutes of severe tearing chest pain radiating through to the interscapular region. She has vomited once.

On examination the right radial pulse is weaker than the left and there is a soft early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. She is neurologically intact.

Vital signs: pulse 108, blood pressure 176/94 right arm and 158/86 left arm, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 97% in room air, temperature 36.5. Electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia with no ST changes. Chest x ray shows a widened mediastinum. Troponin is mildly elevated. CT aortogram demonstrates an intimal flap originating in the aortic root and extending through the aortic arch to the descending thoracic aorta with a small pericardial effusion.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 176/94 right arm and 158/86 left arm, RR 22, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.5
data_table.Examination: Weaker right radial pulse than left; soft early diastolic murmur at left sternal edge; neurologically intact
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia no ST changes; CXR widened mediastinum; troponin mildly elevated
data_table.CT aortogram: Intimal flap from aortic root through arch to descending thoracic aorta; small pericardial effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Intravenous esmolol infusion titrated to heart rate 60 with intravenous glyceryl trinitrate added for medical management alone with no immediate surgical referral for aortic repair
options.rationale: Medical management alone is the primary strategy for uncomplicated type B dissection; type A dissection with root involvement and new aortic regurgitation requires immediate surgery (Source: European Society of Cardiology aortic disease guideline).
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology aortic disease guideline

options.text: Emergency percutaneous coronary intervention because the mildly elevated troponin and interscapular chest pain indicate an acute coronary syndrome as the most likely diagnosis
options.rationale: Mild troponin elevation with a dissection flap indicates dynamic coronary ostial compromise; PCI in an ascending aortic dissection is contraindicated because antiplatelet loading and coronary intervention can worsen dissection and haemopericardium (Source: European Society of Cardiology aortic disease guideline).
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology aortic disease guideline

options.text: Emergency pericardiocentesis for tamponade decompression before proceeding with any imaging or surgical referral for definitive management of the dissection
options.rationale: Pericardiocentesis in type A dissection with tamponade risks acute rebleeding and worse haemodynamic collapse; if attempted at all it is a small volume bridge to the operating theatre, not a first line intervention (Source: European Society of Cardiology aortic disease guideline).
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology aortic disease guideline

options.text: Immediate cardiothoracic surgical referral for emergency open aortic root and arch repair with intravenous esmolol commenced concurrently to control heart rate and blood pressure
options.rationale: This is a Stanford type A dissection (involves the aortic root proximal to the left subclavian) with new aortic regurgitation and pericardial effusion. Type A dissection is a surgical emergency because untreated mortality is around 1 to 2% per hour in the first 48 hours. Concurrent intravenous beta blockade (esmolol) provides rate and pressure control while the theatre is prepared (Source: European Society of Cardiology aortic disease guideline; ANZSCTS aortic surgery guidance).
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology aortic disease guideline

options.text: Commence intravenous unfractionated heparin infusion to a target activated partial thromboplastin time ratio between 2 and 3 while awaiting cardiothoracic surgical opinion
options.rationale: Anticoagulation in acute aortic dissection worsens haemorrhagic complications including cardiac tamponade and is contraindicated (Source: European Society of Cardiology aortic disease guideline).
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology aortic disease guideline

explanation.summary: Stanford type A dissection (any involvement proximal to the left subclavian, including root or arch) is a surgical emergency because complications include coronary ostial compromise, aortic regurgitation, tamponade, and rupture. Type B dissection (originating distal to the left subclavian) is medically managed unless complicated. Pulse and pressure asymmetry, new aortic regurgitation, and pericardial effusion here confirm type A.
key_points: Type A: surgical emergency (root or arch involvement).
Type B: medical unless complicated (malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain).
Beta blocker before any vasodilator in both types.
explanation.pearls: Any dissection reaching the coronary ostia can present with an inferior STEMI pattern. Always check pulse and pressure symmetry and listen for aortic regurgitation before lysing a suspected STEMI in tearing chest pain.

sources.label: European Society of Cardiology aortic disease guideline

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing ACTH dependent from ACTH independent Cushing syndrome
stem:
You are the endocrine registrar. A 46 year old woman with confirmed hypercortisolism has completed all three first line screens for Cushing syndrome. An overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test failed to suppress serum cortisol below 50 nmol/L, 24 hour urinary free cortisol was elevated on two collections, and late night salivary cortisol was elevated.

She now attends for the next step of workup. She has moon face, purple abdominal striae, and proximal weakness. She is on no exogenous steroid and no oral contraceptive.

A morning plasma adrenocorticotrophic hormone concentration returns at 76 ng/L (reference range up to 46 ng/L). No imaging has yet been performed. Renal function and electrolytes are within normal limits.

data_table.Screening tests: Overnight 1 mg DST failed to suppress serum cortisol below 50 nmol/L; 24 h urinary free cortisol elevated on two collections; late night salivary cortisol elevated
data_table.Examination: Moon face; purple abdominal striae; proximal weakness
data_table.Drugs: No exogenous steroid; no oral contraceptive
data_table.ACTH: Morning plasma ACTH 76 ng/L (reference up to 46)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Computed tomography of the adrenal glands with a dedicated adrenal protocol to identify an adenoma or a carcinoma as the source of the confirmed hypercortisolism
options.rationale: Adrenal imaging is the next step in adrenocorticotrophic hormone independent Cushing syndrome (suppressed adrenocorticotrophic hormone); with elevated adrenocorticotrophic hormone the source lies in the pituitary or an ectopic tumour (Source: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for Cushing syndrome).
source_refs: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for Cushing syndrome

options.text: Computed tomography of the chest with dedicated thin slices to identify a small cell lung cancer or a carcinoid as the ectopic source of the confirmed hypercortisolism
options.rationale: Ectopic source imaging (chest and abdomen CT and 68 gallium DOTATATE PET) is pursued after inferior petrosal sinus sampling identifies non pituitary source, not as the initial step after adrenocorticotrophic hormone dependence is confirmed (Source: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for Cushing syndrome).
source_refs: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for Cushing syndrome

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary with dedicated dynamic contrast sequences and consider inferior petrosal sinus sampling if imaging is negative or equivocal
options.rationale: Elevated adrenocorticotrophic hormone confirms adrenocorticotrophic hormone dependent Cushing syndrome. The next step is pituitary MRI with dynamic contrast because approximately 70% of cases are Cushing disease (pituitary adenoma). If MRI is normal or equivocal, or if biochemical features suggest ectopic secretion, inferior petrosal sinus sampling with corticotrophin releasing hormone stimulation localises the source (Source: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for Cushing syndrome).
source_refs: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for Cushing syndrome

options.text: High dose 8 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test as the discriminator between pituitary and ectopic source without the need for pituitary imaging as the next investigation
options.rationale: High dose dexamethasone suppression testing has been largely superseded by inferior petrosal sinus sampling because of imperfect specificity; imaging plus IPSS is the preferred pathway (Source: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for Cushing syndrome).
source_refs: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for Cushing syndrome

options.text: Repeat the 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test to confirm the screening result before pursuing adrenocorticotrophic hormone measurement or definitive imaging
options.rationale: Two of three concordant screening tests already confirm hypercortisolism; repeating a third screen delays care rather than advancing localisation (Source: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for Cushing syndrome).
source_refs: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for Cushing syndrome

explanation.summary: Cushing syndrome workup pathway: (1) confirm hypercortisolism with two concordant screens; (2) measure plasma adrenocorticotrophic hormone to classify as dependent or independent; (3a) if dependent (elevated), image the pituitary and use inferior petrosal sinus sampling if MRI is negative or equivocal; (3b) if independent (suppressed), image the adrenals with a dedicated protocol.
key_points: Elevated ACTH: pituitary MRI +/- inferior petrosal sinus sampling.
Suppressed ACTH: adrenal CT with dedicated protocol.
Ectopic source workup follows negative pituitary sampling.
explanation.pearls: Cyclical Cushing syndrome can give discordant screening results. When suspicion is high but tests are negative, repeat testing over months rather than abandoning the diagnosis.

sources.label: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline for Cushing syndrome

subtopic_detail: Calcium replacement during massive transfusion
stem:
You are the intensive care registrar. A 42 year old woman is undergoing active massive transfusion for postpartum haemorrhage on the theatre table. She has received 6 units of packed red cells, 6 units of fresh frozen plasma, and 1 unit of platelets in the last 45 minutes.

She remains on noradrenaline 0.2 micrograms/kg/minute. The obstetric team continues to actively bleed. Body temperature is 35.1. Blood is warmed on delivery. She has no known cardiac history.

Current point of care values: ionised calcium 0.82 mmol/L (reference 1.10-1.32), potassium 4.6 mmol/L, magnesium 0.72 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), fibrinogen 1.4 g/L (2.0-4.0), pH 7.24, lactate 4.4 mmol/L. Electrocardiogram monitor shows a QTc of 520 ms with occasional ventricular ectopy. No arrhythmia is currently sustained.

data_table.Products in 45 minutes: 6 units packed red cells; 6 units fresh frozen plasma; 1 unit platelets
data_table.Haemodynamics: Noradrenaline 0.2 micrograms/kg/min; active ongoing bleeding; temperature 35.1
data_table.Point of care: Ionised calcium 0.82 mmol/L (1.10-1.32); potassium 4.6; magnesium 0.72 (0.70-1.10); fibrinogen 1.4 g/L (2.0-4.0); pH 7.24; lactate 4.4
data_table.ECG: QTc 520 ms; occasional ventricular ectopy; no sustained arrhythmia
data_table.Background: No known cardiac history; blood warmed on delivery

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Give magnesium sulfate 10 mmol intravenously over 20 minutes as the priority correction because the QT interval prolongation on monitor is driven primarily by hypomagnesaemia
options.rationale: The magnesium of 0.72 is within reference range and the QT prolongation is more likely driven by severe ionised hypocalcaemia; calcium correction is the priority (Source: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines

options.text: Give sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol intravenously to correct the acidosis before proceeding with any further calcium replacement therapy during the ongoing resuscitation
options.rationale: Bicarbonate infusion further lowers ionised calcium (shifts to protein bound fraction) and can worsen the arrhythmia risk; treat the ionised calcium first while correcting the primary haemorrhage (Source: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines

options.text: Give calcium chloride 10 mL of 10% solution intravenously over 5 to 10 minutes with continued transfusion and repeat ionised calcium measurement in 10 minutes
options.rationale: Citrate in blood products chelates ionised calcium and produces symptomatic hypocalcaemia during massive transfusion. Ionised calcium below 0.9 mmol/L is associated with cardiac dysfunction, worsened coagulopathy, and vasoplegia. Calcium chloride 10 mL of 10% (or calcium gluconate 30 mL of 10%) is given intravenously, and ionised calcium is rechecked after every 4 units of red cells during ongoing massive transfusion (Source: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines

options.text: Escalate noradrenaline to 0.4 micrograms/kg/minute as the priority intervention for the vasoplegia driven by systemic inflammatory response secondary to massive transfusion
options.rationale: Escalating vasopressor without correcting ionised calcium leaves the drug ineffective because calcium is required for adrenergic receptor coupling; correct calcium first, then reassess pressor requirement (Source: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines

options.text: Give cryoprecipitate 10 units for the fibrinogen of 1.4 g/L before any calcium replacement because fibrinogen level below 2 g/L drives the ongoing coagulopathy in this presentation
options.rationale: Cryoprecipitate for fibrinogen below 2 g/L is appropriate but calcium replacement is the more time critical intervention because hypocalcaemia causes acute arrhythmia and vasoplegia; both can be given but calcium first (Source: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines).
source_refs: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines

explanation.summary: During massive transfusion, citrate chelates ionised calcium and produces symptomatic hypocalcaemia within minutes. Ionised calcium below 0.9 mmol/L drives arrhythmia, cardiac dysfunction, coagulopathy, and vasoplegia. Give calcium chloride 10 mL of 10% or calcium gluconate 30 mL of 10% intravenously and recheck after every 4 units of red cells.
key_points: Citrate lowers ionised calcium; recheck after every 4 units.
Calcium chloride 10 mL of 10% or calcium gluconate 30 mL of 10%.
Correct calcium before escalating pressor or giving bicarbonate.
explanation.pearls: The lethal triad in massive transfusion is often taught as hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy. Hypocalcaemia is the fourth silent contributor and the easiest to miss without point of care testing.

sources.label: National Blood Authority Patient Blood Management Guidelines
